A 47-year-old woman seeks medical attention for a 5-day history of dull pelvic pain that began following
a fall onto her buttocks. Her medical history includes generalized anxiety disorder and chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease, with current medications including citalopram, tiotropium, and albuterol.
Acetaminophen has not provided pain relief. Physical examination reveals stable vital signs (BP 138/86
mm Hg, HR 80/min, RR 14/min, temperature 37.2°C) and a 3/6 systolic murmur at the apex. While
imaging shows no acute fracture or dislocation, osteopathic structural examination reveals the following
findings: elevated anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) on the right, lowered posterior superior iliac spine
(PSIS) on the left, lowered ischial tuberosity on the left, and a positive standing flexion test on the right.
What is the most likely diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Bilateral sacral torsion (B) Left inferior shear
(C) Left anterior innominate rotation (D) Right superior shear (E) Right posterior innominate rotation (F)
Left posterior rotation (G) Bilateral iliosacral dysfunction (H) Right anterior rotation (I) Right innominate
upslip (J) Left sacroiliac joint dysfunction
 A. Right superior shear
B. Right anterior rotation
C. Right posterior innominate rotation
D. Bilateral sacral torsion
E. Left sacroiliac joint dysfunction
F. Bilateral iliosacral dysfunction
G. Left posterior rotation
H. Left anterior innominate rotation
I. Left inferior shear
J. Right innominate upslip
